headline: High risk: shared filesystem and broad write/network privileges create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and cascading-error pathways by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and both share state via the filesystem/clipboard, so attacker-controlled content from one can be consumed by the other as instructions. Open Interpreter’s manual desktop automation and Windsurf’s MCP/file-based workflow make this plausible in default use, though not as directly as a shared MCP server. The pathway exists without unusual setup.
conditions: IF either agent reads a file produced by the other without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF clipboard copy-paste is used between the agents, malicious instructions can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable clipboard bridging between agents.
Keep each agent in a separate workspace directory.
Require manual review of any file before the other agent reads it.
Turn off auto-run / auto-execute features.
Use provenance labels in filenames and comments.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open Interpreter can access the entire user filesystem and broad network egress, while Windsurf reads workspace files and can send content to its model proxy/MCP servers. Because both share filesystem-based state, sensitive local data touched by A can flow into B’s outputs or upstream APIs in default workflows. This is a realistic leakage path, though not enough for critical without explicit PHI/secret scope.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace or reachable filesystem, both agents can access them.
IF Windsurf forwards workspace content to its model proxy or MCP server, data can leave the local machine.
mitigations: Restrict both agents to a minimal project directory.
Remove secrets from the shared workspace before use.
Disable or limit network egress for the more privileged agent.
Use separate OS accounts for each agent.
Audit which files each agent opened before allowing further runs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, package installation, and git-state modification, and both share state via the local filesystem. That creates a direct race/conflict pathway where each can overwrite the other’s edits or corrupt git state without locking. The default concurrency model is therefore dangerous and can cause irreversible repository damage.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF either agent modifies git state while the other is active, history or working-tree corruption can occur.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time in a shared repo.
Use separate clones for each agent.
Disable auto-commit or auto-merge behaviors.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel use.
Add file-locking or orchestration locks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Windsurf’s Cascade loop can treat prior agent output as actionable context, and Open Interpreter can generate code, commands, or file edits that Windsurf may then continue without independent verification. Because both have execution authority, a mistaken or malicious output from A can cascade into B’s actions and amplify damage. This is a default-pathway risk, not a niche configuration issue.
conditions: IF Windsurf consumes Open Interpreter output as authoritative, errors can propagate into subsequent actions.
IF Open Interpreter emits commands or patches that Windsurf applies automatically, the cascade can execute harmful changes.
mitigations: Require human review between agents.
Force Windsurf to verify diffs before applying them.
Disable auto-run / auto-execute on both agents.
Limit Open Interpreter to read-only analysis for the first pass.
Log and compare proposed actions before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not specify regulated-data certifications or residency mismatches. The only concrete compliance concern is that Open Interpreter can touch anything on the local machine while Windsurf handles workspace files and may send content to model proxy/MCP services, so a policy mismatch is possible but not evidenced. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace, policy review is required before use.
IF Windsurf routes regulated content to external model services, a residency or retention mismatch may occur.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the shared workspace.
Check vendor retention and residency settings before use.
Use a local-only model path where possible.
Separate regulated projects from general-purpose automation.
Document the data classes each agent may touch.
